terms.definition: An uptime promise of 99.99%, which allows only 52.6 minutes of unplanned outage a year — about 4.4 minutes a month — against the 8.8 hours a 99.9% tier permits.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client in a business-services roleplay demands a tighter guarantee, you have to convert each tier into allowed downtime minutes before you can price the upgrade or refuse it.

terms.definition: The period over which uptime is averaged before credits are computed; a four-hour outage breaches a daily window but disappears inside a monthly average, so the window length decides whether the same failure costs the vendor anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward the competitor who asks how availability is measured rather than only what percentage is promised, because the window is where a generous-looking SLA is quietly defanged.

terms.definition: A contractual clock that runs until the client's issue is actually fixed rather than merely acknowledged, so a vendor can meet a 15-minute acknowledgement promise and still breach a four-hour fix promise on the same ticket.
terms.whyItMatters: Support-contract roleplays hinge on separating the two clocks; quoting one response number when the client is complaining about repair speed reads as evasion to a judge.

terms.definition: Hours charged to clients divided by hours available in the period; on a 2,000-hour year a consultant at 75% bills 1,500 hours, so each point lost is roughly 20 hours of revenue that cannot be recovered later.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and hiring questions on a services exam are settled with this ratio — you cannot argue for another consultant without showing the current team's utilization.

terms.definition: Dollars actually collected divided by the dollars standard rates would have produced; a firm billing 1,500 hours at $200 but collecting $255,000 realizes 85%, with the gap made of write-offs, courtesy hours and negotiated discounts.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains the exam scenario where a fully booked practice still misses its revenue target — the hours were worked and utilization was fine, but they were not all billed.

terms.definition: Client price divided by the delivery staffer's fully loaded cost rate — a $50 cost billed at $150 is a 3.0 multiple, roughly the floor a services firm needs to cover overhead, bench time and still earn a profit.
terms.whyItMatters: A discount request in a B2B selling roleplay is answered with this number: cutting a $150 rate to $110 drops the multiple to 2.2 and eats the margin the firm runs on.

terms.definition: The mix of junior to senior staff carrying an engagement; pushing work down a level lifts margin because juniors bill somewhat less but cost far less, which is why a pyramid-shaped team beats an all-expert team on the same fixed fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing a fixed-fee project in a roleplay means defending the mix to a client who wants only senior people on the account.

terms.definition: A surety instrument worth roughly 5% to 10% of the amount bid, forfeited if the winning bidder walks away or refuses to sign at the price submitted, which is what makes a lowball number costly to withdraw.
terms.whyItMatters: Public-sector and large corporate solicitations require one, so a roleplay about pursuing a government services contract has to account for its cost in the bid decision.

terms.definition: Chained dependencies multiply rather than average, so a service running on a 99.9% platform behind a 99.9% network and a 99.95% payment gateway can honestly promise only 99.75% end to end — roughly 22 hours of outage a year.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants 99.9% guaranteed on a stack you resell is answered by multiplying your vendors' numbers first; promising more than the product is a breach you signed at the outset.

terms.definition: The downtime a target permits, treated as an allowance to spend rather than a line to defend — a 99.9% monthly promise leaves 43.2 minutes, so one 20-minute release failure has already consumed nearly half the month.
terms.whyItMatters: Change-management items on a services exam use it as the trigger: once the budget is spent the vendor freezes releases, which is the concrete answer to when you stop shipping.

terms.definition: Average elapsed time from detection to the service being usable again, and the lever inside availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR); with a failure every 500 hours, cutting restoration from four hours to one moves uptime from 99.2% to 99.8%.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client demands fewer outages in a managed-services roleplay, faster recovery is the cheaper counter-offer, and you need the formula to prove it lands on the same uptime number.

terms.definition: Banded refunds tied to the month's measured uptime — 99.0 to 99.9% returns 10% of the fee, 95 to 99% returns 25%, under 95% returns 50% — so a month at 98.7% on a $40,000 contract owes $10,000 and the band edge, not the outage length, sets the bill.
terms.whyItMatters: Renewal negotiations turn on which band an outage lands in; a competitor who can price the month before conceding a credit keeps the account profitable.

terms.definition: The hours during which response clocks actually run: under 8x5 coverage a severity-one ticket opened at 4 p.m. Friday with a four-hour target is not late until Monday noon, while the identical promise under 24x7 breaches at 8 p.m.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in a support-contract roleplay watch for the competitor who sells the coverage upgrade rather than a tighter number — the clock's hours, not its length, are what the client is complaining about.

terms.definition: Total support spend divided by tickets resolved, a figure that rises when self-service succeeds, because the cheap contacts are the ones deflected and the expensive escalated ones are all that remain in the denominator.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam scenario where automation raised cost per ticket is testing whether you read the mix change instead of calling the deflection program a failure.

terms.definition: Cash actually received divided by the amount invoiced — a different fraction from realization, because a firm can bill 95% of standard rates and still collect only 80% of those invoices, and only the second number funds payroll.
terms.whyItMatters: A cash-squeeze roleplay at a fully booked agency is solved here: the repair is in collections and credit terms, not in selling more hours.

terms.definition: Salary plus payroll taxes, benefits and allocated overhead, divided by the hours a person is genuinely available to bill rather than the 2,080 they are paid for; using the payroll denominator understates true cost by roughly 15 to 20% and prices work below breakeven.
terms.whyItMatters: Every pricing-floor question on a services exam starts here, and quoting a bill rate off unloaded salary in a roleplay ends the sale as soon as a judge asks about benefits.

terms.definition: Signed but undelivered revenue divided by average monthly delivery capacity, read in months — under about three months a firm is hiring into hope, and over six it is quietly turning away work it could have sold.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring recommendation in a business-services roleplay needs this number, because "we're busy" is not evidence a judge accepts for adding headcount.

terms.definition: Hours already delivered but not yet invoiced; add the days they sit unbilled to the days an invoice waits for payment and a monthly billing cycle on net-45 terms funds about 75 days of payroll before the first dollar arrives.
terms.whyItMatters: The cash-flow roleplay at a growing consultancy is won by shortening the billing cycle, which only makes sense once unbilled days and receivable days are counted as one lag.

terms.definition: Booking a share of a fixed fee equal to costs incurred over total estimated costs, which means an overrun mechanically pulls revenue forward: spend 70% of the budget on half the work and the books show 70% earned until the estimate is revised and it reverses.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions about a services firm restating a quarter test whether you know the cost estimate, not the invoice, drives when revenue lands.

terms.definition: Forecast final cost of an engagement: money already spent plus the remaining work divided by the cost performance index, so $60,000 spent with $40,000 of work left at a CPI of 0.8 finishes at $110,000, not the $100,000 in the proposal.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-project roleplays where the client asks whether the budget still holds require this arithmetic before you promise anything you cannot deliver.

terms.definition: Revenue on one project less only its direct delivery cost — loaded labor, travel and subcontractors — before any overhead, so a 40% result at a firm carrying a 35% overhead load leaves five points and is a project worth declining.
terms.whyItMatters: A go/no-go roleplay on a discounted proposal turns on comparing this margin against the overhead load, not on whether the project appears to make money.

terms.definition: The agreed fee divided by the hours the team actually consumed: $48,000 delivered in 320 hours is $150 an hour against a $200 rate card, a 25% erosion that never appears in revenue and shows up only when delivered hours are counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Post-project debriefs on the services exam ask why a profitable-looking fixed fee hurt the year, and this ratio is the evidence a judge expects you to produce.

terms.definition: The hour count at which two pricing structures cost the buyer the same — a $60,000 fee against a $200 blended rate breaks even at 300 hours — so a client whose scope truly needs 250 should refuse the fixed price and one expecting 400 should insist on it.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing roleplays are decided by naming that crossover out loud; recommending a structure without it reads as a preference rather than analysis.

terms.definition: A prepaid bank of hours billed at a discount and forfeited if unused inside the period, unlike an access retainer that buys availability whether or not any work is requested — the expiry, not the discount, is the term worth negotiating.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking to roll over unused hours at renewal is asking you to change which retainer they bought, so you have to know the two are different products before conceding.

terms.definition: Payment set as a share of verified savings above an agreed baseline, which means whoever defines the baseline defines the payout — anchor it on a peak-cost year and the vendor earns a bonus for the client merely reverting to normal spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Outsourcing roleplays that open with "we only pay if you save us money" are won by negotiating the baseline and the measurement method, never the percentage.

terms.definition: A fee computed as a fixed share of whatever the job ends up costing, which pays the provider more for every overrun and is barred outright in federal contracting for exactly that reason; a fee fixed in dollars at award is the lawful version.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-services roleplays require pricing the work in a structure the buyer may legally accept — proposing a percentage of cost disqualifies the bid before the price is compared.

terms.definition: The smallest unit a ticket can bill in, and at a quarter-hour floor forty six-minute calls invoice ten hours against four actually worked, which is why increment size rather than hourly rate often decides whether a support contract earns anything.
terms.whyItMatters: A client disputing an invoice in a roleplay is usually disputing the increment, so you have to reconstruct the bill from ticket counts to answer them.

terms.definition: An endorsement extending the reporting period after a claims-made professional liability policy ends, priced near 100 to 200% of the last annual premium; skip it and work already delivered becomes uninsured the moment the policy lapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling or winding down a services firm in a roleplay means budgeting for it, because past clients can still sue and the buyer's diligence list asks for proof it was purchased.

terms.definition: A smaller cap sitting inside a larger one for a named category of loss, so a $5 million cyber policy carrying a $250,000 social-engineering sublimit pays a quarter of a million on a wire-fraud loss no matter what the headline limit says.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client's contract demands $5 million of cyber coverage, the roleplay answer is to read the sublimits, because that is where the protection they actually need is rationed.

terms.definition: The most an insurer will pay across every claim in a policy year, a separate ceiling from the per-occurrence cap — a $1 million / $2 million policy that pays two full claims in March leaves the client uncovered for the remaining nine months.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-qualification roleplay where the client requires $1 million of errors-and-omissions coverage is answered with both numbers; meeting the per-occurrence figure alone can leave the contract effectively bare.

terms.definition: Card-transaction volume decides which validation a provider must pass: above roughly six million a year forces an on-site assessment by a qualified assessor plus quarterly network scans, while a small e-commerce seller self-assesses on a questionnaire.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-adjacent services roleplay hinges on whether absorbing a client's volume pushes you over the threshold, because the compliance cost, not the processing fee, is what changes.

terms.definition: A signed statement covering the gap between an audit report's period end and the client's fiscal year end — a report closing September 30 needs one for October through December, and most auditors refuse to bridge more than about three months.
terms.whyItMatters: Enterprise procurement roleplays stall exactly here: the client's auditor wants assurance through December and the vendor's only report stops in September.
